Early Saturday, officials said  about 250 homes had been damaged or destroyed. The woman who was killed, Kori Bryant, was at home with her daughter, Olivia, when the tornado struck, said family member Mark McClure. Another family member, who found the mother and daughter after the tornado, said attempts were made to resuscitate the infant, but she couldn't be saved, according to McClure. The baby was found in her car seat. Her parents had put her in the seat, thinking it would be safer for her, McClure said. The Bryants were in the hallway with the baby when the tornado struck. The woman's husband, John Bryant, was found about two houses away, McClure said. His back and ribs were broken, and a lung had collapsed. He was taken to Vanderbilt University Hospital, and he will undergo surgery when his blood pressure stabilizes, McClure said. Just before 1:40 p.m., the tornado hit Murfreesboro in Rutherford County, 30 miles southeast of Nashville, he said. Thirty-six people were treated for tornado-related injuries at Middle Tennessee Medical Center in Murfreesboro, said hospital spokeswoman Martha Tolbert. The search-and-rescue effort was continuing into the evening, Smith said.  Watch damage caused by tornado in Murfreesboro » . Elsewhere in the region, the town of Mena, Arkansas, is cleaning up after a tornado roared through, killing three people and damaging or destroying more than 100 homes, an Arkansas official said. About 50 soldiers also helped with security and food distribution. Mena, population 6,000, took a heavy hit on the west side of town, as the storm swept through downtown before heading up state Highway 71, said Tommy Jackson from the state Department of Emergency Management. "It looks like a war zone out here," said James Reeves, also from the department.  Watch scenes of devastation in Mena » . He said electricity and gas were out in the western half of the city. Two plants at an industrial park were destroyed, said reporter Charles Crowson of CNN affiliate KTHV-TV. A family's split-second decision to shelter their infant daughter in her car seat may have saved the baby's life when a powerful tornado ripped through their community late Tuesday, leveling homes and leaving a trail of devastation that officials are still working to assess.

The tornado, which touched down shortly after 9 p.m., carved a path of destruction nearly a mile wide, flattening dozens of homes and downing power lines across the area. At least seven people were killed and more than 40 injured, according to local emergency management officials.

Among the survivors was the Hernandez family, who took refuge in an interior bathroom as the storm bore down on their single-story home.

"We heard it coming — it sounded like a freight train," said Maria Hernandez, 34, speaking from a hospital bed where she was being treated for a broken arm and lacerations. "We just grabbed the baby, put her in the car seat, and covered her with our bodies and a mattress. That's all we could think to do."

"The car seat likely absorbed a tremendous amount of impact," said Dr. Alan Whitmore, an emergency physician treating storm victims. "In situations like this, the padding and harness system can make an extraordinary difference for a small child."

"These men and women are working around the clock in difficult and dangerous conditions," said National Guard Sgt. Daniel Foster. "We've pulled several people from collapsed structures already, and we're not done yet."

## A Community Reeling

As dawn broke, the scale of the destruction became clear. Cars were tossed like toys, trees were stripped bare, and entire blocks were reduced to piles of splintered wood and twisted metal.

Utility crews estimated that thousands of residents remained without power, and officials urged people to stay away from the hardest-hit areas to allow emergency vehicles to move freely.

The American Red Cross has established shelters for those left homeless, and donation centers are being organized to collect food, water and supplies.

For the Hernandez family, gratitude has overshadowed their injuries.
